semantics: Launch set of the Evidence-Graded Claims Library (portfolio plan 3.4), free public summaries only; gated depth waits for membership infrastructure. Two axes: grade_strength (strong | moderate | limited | insufficient | contradicted) describes the evidence for the claim as parents state it; grade_consensus (consensus | majority | divided | fringe) describes where the field sits. The claims grader enforces: every claim fully fielded, at least two sources each, hedging language present wherever strength is limited or insufficient, no overclaim vocabulary above the grade, reading level, and enum validity. Per the production pipeline, the model proposes and Matthew disposes: grades carry drafted status until his review flips it (keel/REVIEW.md).

claims.claim_text: Hearing two languages will confuse my baby and delay their speech.
claims.verdict_label: Bilingual children babble on time, and their vocabulary is on track when you count both languages.
claims.summary_public: The confusion myth is one of the clearest cases in this library, and the developmental science field is unusually united here. Babies raised hearing two languages start babbling at about the same age as other babies, and their total vocabulary across both languages is on par with children learning one. In any single language they may know fewer words or use simpler sentences for a while, which is expected and not a delay. That is why how you count matters: their vocabulary lives across both languages, so measuring one language against monolingual norms undercounts them. Code-mixing, using both languages in one sentence, is not confusion. Bilingual adults mix in systematic, grammatical ways, and bilingual children's mixing follows rules much like theirs. Parents mixing languages in their own speech also appears, on current evidence, to be mostly unrelated to children's vocabulary, apart from a small, uncertain link with understanding words in the community language. Clinical reviews describe two practical harms of this myth. Some families are advised to drop a home language to help speech, but that advice is not supported by the science, may do less for the child's other language than hoped, and gives up a language that research links to stronger family relationships. Clinicians can also misread a bilingual child in either direction: sometimes mistaking normal bilingual development for a delay, and sometimes missing a real delay because it gets put down to bilingualism. The red lines for a language conversation with your pediatrician are the same for bilingual children as for anyone, counted across all languages.

sources.citation: Byers-Heinlein K, Lew-Williams C. Bilingualism in the early years: what the science says. LEARNing Landscapes. 2013;7(1):95-112.
sources.role: Research review: no confusion; code-mixing follows rules; total vocabulary

sources.citation: Hoff E, Core C. What clinicians need to know about bilingual development. Seminars in Speech and Language. 2015;36(2):89-99.
sources.role: Clinical guidance: count total vocabulary; do not discourage the home language

sources.citation: Oller DK, Eilers RE, Urbano R, Cobo-Lewis AB. Development of precursors to speech in infants exposed to two languages. Journal of Child Language. 1997;24(2):407-425.
sources.role: Longitudinal study of 73 infants: babbling begins at similar ages in bilingual and monolingual infants

sources.citation: Hoff E, Core C, Place S, et al. Dual language exposure and early bilingual development. Journal of Child Language. 2012;39(1):1-27.
sources.role: Behind in single-language comparisons, comparable in total vocabulary

sources.role: Evidence synthesis: parental mixing mostly unrelated to vocabulary

claims.claim_text: A baby walker will help my baby learn to walk sooner.
claims.verdict_label: Walkers don't help babies walk sooner, and the injury record led the AAP to call for a ban.
claims.summary_public: This one earns the library's rarest combination: the product does not deliver its named benefit, and it carries a documented injury cost. Studies comparing babies who used walkers with babies who did not found that walker babies did not walk sooner. One study found they sat, crawled, and walked later and scored lower on development tests. Those studies were not randomized, and a review found research in this area generally low in quality, with motor delays that were mostly temporary. So the delay is less certain than the lack of benefit. One study's authors suggested a reason: a walker blocks a baby's view of their own legs as they move. Time in a walker may also take the place of floor play. Meanwhile, walkers give pre-walking babies speed and reach they cannot control. An estimated 230,000 US children under 15 months were treated in emergency rooms for walker injuries between 1990 and 2014, about three in four from falls down stairs. These numbers back the American Academy of Pediatrics' call for a ban on making and selling walkers. Injuries fell after a 2010 US safety standard, but walkers are still sold there. Canada banned them in 2004. A stationary activity center gives the upright time without the wheels. Floor time is how babies build these skills. If a walker is already in your house, keep it far from any stairs and make sure there is plenty of floor time too.

sources.citation: Siegel AC, Burton RV. Effects of baby walkers on motor and mental development in human infants. Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics. 1999;20(5):355-361.
sources.role: Observational comparison: walker infants sat, crawled, and walked later

sources.citation: American Academy of Pediatrics, Committee on Injury and Poison Prevention. Injuries associated with infant walkers. Pediatrics. 2001;108(3):790-792.
sources.role: Injury data and the AAP's call for a ban

sources.citation: Sims A, Chounthirath T, Yang J, Hodges NL, Smith GA. Infant walker-related injuries in the United States. Pediatrics. 2018;142(4):e20174332.

claims.claim_text: Tummy time actually matters for my baby's development.
claims.verdict_label: Yes: awake tummy time is linked to better motor development; the head-shape evidence is mixed.
claims.summary_public: Tummy time is standard baby advice with a systematic review behind it. Across 16 studies of over 4,000 infants, more awake tummy time was linked to better gross motor development, including rolling and crawling, and to less flattening across the back of the head. The findings for flattening on one side were mixed. The honest grading note: most of the underlying studies are observational, so the strength here is moderate rather than strong; babies who get more floor time may differ from babies who don't in other ways too. But the direction is consistent for skills like rolling and crawling, and the practice costs nothing. What the evidence does not support is tummy-time guilt. The World Health Organization suggests at least 30 minutes a day, spread across the day, for babies who are not yet moving on their own. The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests starting with 3 to 5 minutes, two or three times a day, and working up to 15 to 30 minutes a day by about 7 weeks. Short, frequent sessions are how most babies get there. If your baby fusses, try a change: lie back and set them on your chest so they can see your face, or put yourself or a toy within reach.

sources.citation: Hewitt L, Kerr E, Stanley RM, Okely AD. Tummy time and infant health outcomes: a systematic review. Pediatrics. 2020;145(6):e20192168.
sources.role: Systematic review, 16 studies: linked to better gross motor development and less flattening across the back of the head; findings for one-sided flattening unclear

sources.citation: World Health Organization. Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2019.
sources.role: At least 30 minutes of awake prone time a day for babies not yet mobile

sources.citation: Moon RY, Carlin RF, Hand I; Task Force on Sudden Infant Death Syndrome and the Committee on Fetus and Newborn. Sleep-related infant deaths: updated 2022 recommendations for reducing infant deaths in the sleep environment. Pediatrics. 2022;150(1):e2022057990.
sources.role: Current AAP safe-sleep policy: supervised, awake tummy time

sources.citation: American Academy of Pediatrics. Back to Sleep, Tummy to Play. HealthyChildren.org. Last updated September 8, 2026.
sources.role: Parent guidance: 3 to 5 minutes, two or three times a day, working up to 15 to 30 minutes by 7 weeks

claims.claim_text: Screen time is harming my toddler's language development.
claims.verdict_label: Heavy, passive, background screen use is linked to less language input; the dose and the type matter more than the screen.
claims.summary_public: The screen-time literature rewards precision, because the honest answer depends on what is actually happening. A large Canadian study of children aged 2 to 5 and a 2020 review of 42 studies both find that more screen time is linked to somewhat lower language and developmental scores. The links are small. There is some direct evidence for one likely reason: screens may crowd out the back-and-forth talk that builds language. In a lab study, background TV reduced both how much and how well parents talked and played with their young children, and a study that recorded family days found that more screen time went with fewer adult words and fewer conversational turns. Young toddlers also tend to learn less from video than from a live person. Researchers call this the video deficit, and it shrinks as children get older. What the same literature does not support is panic over moderate, co-viewed use. In one small study, toddlers who video chatted live with a new adult later recognized that adult and learned more new patterns than toddlers who watched the same adult on recorded video, though a larger review did not find live video consistently better. Watching alongside an adult is linked to better language, not worse. These are also mostly associations; families with heavy screen use differ in many other ways, which is why the strength grade is moderate. The practical read: protect daily stretches of screen-free back-and-forth, cut background TV first, and worry less about the occasional co-watched show.

sources.citation: Madigan S, McArthur BA, Anhorn C, Eirich R, Christakis DA. Associations between screen use and child language skills: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. 2020;174(7):665-675.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: more screen time and background TV linked to weaker language; co-viewing linked to stronger

sources.citation: Madigan S, Browne D, Racine N, Mori C, Tough S. Association between screen time and children's performance on a developmental screening test. JAMA Pediatrics. 2019;173(3):244-250.
sources.role: Longitudinal: more screen hours preceded lower scores on a whole-development screen

sources.citation: Kirkorian HL, Pempek TA, Murphy LA, Schmidt ME, Anderson DR. The impact of background television on parent-child interaction. Child Development. 2009;80(5):1350-1359.

sources.role: Small experiment (60 toddlers): live video chat led to partner recognition and more pattern learning than prerecorded video; more word learning only in the oldest

claims.claim_text: Pacifier use will delay my child's speech.
claims.verdict_label: There is not enough evidence that ordinary pacifier use delays speech; the clearer tradeoffs are ear infections and, with long use, teeth.
claims.summary_public: For ordinary pacifier use in the first couple of years, the evidence for speech harm is weak. The studies are few, small, and mixed, and a 2021 systematic review called the evidence inconsistent and inconclusive. No solid body of research shows that typical pacifier use delays speech or language development. The honest grade is simply that we do not have enough evidence, and the loud warnings outrun the data. The most consistent signal, still weak, is that longer-lasting sucking habits, from a pacifier or a thumb, have been linked to speech-sound problems in three of the four studies the review found. One study of 100 children found that those who used a pacifier more often during the day made more unusual speech-sound errors, a link seen only in the younger children (under about three), and the authors note these errors may resolve over time. What the literature does document is different and worth knowing. Pacifier use is associated with more ear infections, and guidance suggests cutting back in the second half of the first year for that reason. Use that continues past about age two is associated with dental changes, which become more marked after about age four. There is also a protective association with SIDS when a pacifier is offered at sleep, which is why safe-sleep guidance recommends offering one. If you are breastfeeding, current safe-sleep guidance says to wait until breastfeeding is firmly established, meaning a good milk supply, a comfortable latch, and healthy weight gain, before offering a pacifier; how long that takes varies from baby to baby. The pragmatic read fits this evidence: keeping the pacifier for sleep and soothing, rather than all day, may be a sensible middle path, and weaning by about age two or three may help limit the dental effects, which grow the longer use continues.

sources.citation: Burr S, Harding S, Wren Y, Deave T. The relationship between feeding and non-nutritive sucking behaviours and speech sound development: a systematic review. Folia Phoniatrica et Logopaedica. 2021;73(2):75-88.
sources.role: Systematic review: evidence inconsistent and inconclusive; long sucking habits the most consistent signal

sources.citation: Strutt C, Khattab G, Willoughby J. Does the duration and frequency of dummy (pacifier) use affect the development of speech? International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders. 2021;56(3):512-527.
sources.role: Most speech outcomes unrelated; frequent daytime use linked to atypical errors in younger children

sources.citation: Sexton S, Natale R. Risks and benefits of pacifiers. American Family Physician. 2009;79(8):681-685.
sources.role: Clinical review: ear infections, SIDS, and dental effects

sources.citation: Nelson AM. A comprehensive review of evidence and current recommendations related to pacifier usage. Journal of Pediatric Nursing. 2012;27(6):690-699.
sources.role: Review of benefits and risks: soothing, SIDS, ear infections, breastfeeding, teeth

claims.claim_text: Talking to my baby, even before they can respond, builds their language.
claims.verdict_label: Yes. Talking with your baby builds language, and back-and-forth exchanges look especially important.
claims.summary_public: This is one of the best-supported ideas in early language research, with one modern refinement. Decades of research link the talk children hear to their language skills, and a 2021 meta-analysis found that both the amount and the quality of parents' talk are linked to children's language, with quality, meaning varied words and fuller sentences, the stronger link. The famous '30 million word gap' made the finding a headline, but that number comes from one small study of families recorded in the 1980s and has been fairly criticized; later work finds the gap is smaller and depends on what is counted. Newer studies that record a whole day at home suggest that back-and-forth exchanges, where you respond to your baby and give them a turn, may matter even more than the total number of words. In one long-term study, more of these exchanges at 18 to 24 months went with stronger language and IQ scores about ten years later, even after accounting for the mother's education level. A smaller brain-imaging study of 4- to 6-year-olds found a similar pattern in language areas of the brain. And in a randomized trial, coaching parents of 6-month-olds to use parentese, the slower, higher-pitched, sing-song style, and to take turns led to more back-and-forth exchanges and stronger language skills by 18 months. These studies rely on automated counts that are imperfect, so the exact size of the effect is still being worked out. The practical translation is freeing: you do not need to monologue all day or perform enrichment. Talking to your baby helps, and responding to your baby seems to help even more: treat their sounds, gestures, and eventually words as turns, answer them, and wait for the next one. Every tool on this site that touches language is built on this idea.

sources.citation: Anderson NJ, Graham SA, Prime H, Jenkins JM, Madigan S. Linking quality and quantity of parental linguistic input to child language skills: a meta-analysis. Child Development. 2021;92(2):484-501.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: both quantity and quality of parent talk linked to language; quality more strongly

sources.citation: Dailey S, Bergelson E. Language input to infants of different socioeconomic statuses: a quantitative meta-analysis. Developmental Science. 2022;25(3):e13192.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: the word gap is smaller than the original figure and depends on what is counted

claims.verdict_label: Teething can nudge temperature up slightly; a real fever should not be blamed on teeth.
claims.summary_public: Several studies that tracked babies day by day, and reviews that pooled them, point the same way. Teething is genuinely associated with gum irritation, drooling, fussiness, and a slight rise in temperature around eruption days. Most studies have not found a link to fever in the medical sense, which usually means 38C (100.4F) or higher. In a large study that tracked 125 infants every day, temperatures over 102F were not more common around teething. One review found a possible link only with rectal readings, and the studies have real limits, which is why the field's agreement is graded as a majority view rather than full consensus. The American Academy of Pediatrics states that teething does not cause fever. Why this matters more than it seems: teething happens on and off for two years, which makes it an easy explanation for almost any symptom. The bigger risk is attribution error. A baby with a real fever who is assumed to be 'just teething' may have an illness that is being explained away by a coincidence of timing. The evidence-based rule is worth keeping. Fussiness, gnawing, and drool with a barely raised temperature fits teething. An actual fever means treat the child as sick, and call your pediatrician if you would have called for that fever anyway, teeth or no teeth.

sources.citation: Massignan C, Cardoso M, Porporatti AL, et al. Signs and symptoms of primary tooth eruption: a meta-analysis. Pediatrics. 2016;137(3):e20153501.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: eruption brings a slight temperature rise, not characterized as fever

sources.citation: Macknin ML, Piedmonte M, Jacobs J, Skibinski C. Symptoms associated with infant teething: a prospective study. Pediatrics. 2000;105(4 Pt 1):747-752.
sources.role: Day-by-day study of 125 infants: mild rise, no link with high fever; warns against blaming illness on teeth

sources.citation: Nemezio MA, de Oliveira KMH, Romualdo PC, et al. Association between fever and primary tooth eruption: a systematic review and meta-analysis. International Journal of Clinical Pediatric Dentistry. 2017;10(3):293-298.
sources.role: Meta-analysis: no overall link with fever; a possible link with rectal readings

sources.citation: American Academy of Pediatrics. Teething Pain. HealthyChildren.org. Updated July 2025.
sources.role: The AAP's parent guidance: teething does not cause fever

sources.citation: Markman L. Teething: facts and fiction. Pediatrics in Review. 2009;30(8):e59-e64.
sources.role: Clinical review of teething beliefs

claims.claim_text: Baby-led weaning is better than spoon-feeding purées.
claims.verdict_label: A reasonable option, not a clearly better one; the few trials so far show mixed results on growth.
claims.summary_public: Baby-led weaning arrived with big claims: better self-regulation, less picky eating, lower obesity risk. When a modified version of baby-led weaning was tested in a randomized trial, the BLISS study, babies' body mass index and overweight rates did not differ clearly from spoon-fed babies at one or two years. A second trial, in Turkey, found baby-led babies were a little lighter at one year, about 0.7 kg on average, so the growth picture is mixed. Choking was no more common in the baby-led group when families were taught how to prepare safer foods, but about a third of all babies in the trial choked at least once between 6 and 8 months, so safe preparation matters whichever way you feed. Iron levels were similar when parents were advised to offer an iron-rich food at every meal. Evidence on pickiness and appetite is mixed. In the trial, parents reported less fussiness at one year, but most of this evidence relies on parent reports, and families who choose baby-led weaning often differ in other ways. So the honest grade is limited: not contradicted, not established, and a 2026 review of the trials reached the same cautious reading. The practical translation is unusually low-stakes. Both roads lead to a toddler who eats table food. Pick the one that fits your household, mix them freely, and spend the reclaimed worry elsewhere.

sources.citation: Taylor RW, Williams SM, Fangupo LJ, et al. Effect of a baby-led approach to complementary feeding on infant growth and overweight: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Pediatrics. 2017;171(9):838-846.
sources.role: The BLISS trial (a modified baby-led approach): no clear difference in growth at 12 and 24 months

sources.citation: Fangupo LJ, Heath AM, Williams SM, et al. A baby-led approach to eating solids and risk of choking. Pediatrics. 2016;138(4):e20160772.
sources.role: BLISS choking outcome: no group difference; 35% of all infants choked at least once between 6 and 8 months

sources.citation: Daniels L, Taylor RW, Williams SM, et al. Impact of a modified version of baby-led weaning on iron intake and status: a randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. 2018;8(6):e019036.
sources.role: Iron intake and status similar with advice to offer iron-rich food at each meal

sources.citation: Dogan E, Yilmaz G, Caylan N, et al. Baby-led complementary feeding: randomized controlled study. Pediatrics International. 2018;60(12):1073-1080.
sources.role: Second trial (280 infants): baby-led infants about 0.7 kg lighter at 12 months

sources.citation: Márquez-Díaz RR, Ruíz-Fernández MD, Arcas-Rueda M, et al. Baby-led weaning vs traditional spoon-feeding: a systematic review of infant growth, choking risk, and iron status among infants aged 6-12 months. Nutrition Reviews. 2026. doi:10.1093/nutrit/nuaf288.

sources.role: Review of the early, mostly observational evidence: possible benefits, but weak conclusions

claims.claim_text: Reading to my toddler actually changes their language development.
claims.verdict_label: Yes. Reading together builds language, and reading interactively, with questions and pauses, can add to the benefit.
claims.summary_public: Shared book reading is one of the most-studied parent behaviors in developmental science, and it holds up. A 2020 meta-analysis of randomized trials found that shared reading programs modestly improve children's language, with larger effects on the words children say than on the words they understand, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends reading with children from infancy. One practical finding, though not every review confirms it, is about how you read. In the original dialogic reading study, parents were taught to turn reading into a conversation: ask open questions, expand on what the child says, and read less straight from the page. In that first small study of about 30 families, toddlers whose parents learned this style scored months ahead on tests of the words they used after about a month, and the gap narrowed later; later studies found smaller but still real benefits. A 2008 review found the added benefit of the interactive style was clearest for 2- and 3-year-olds. It was smaller for 4- and 5-year-olds and for children at risk for language problems, though two later reviews did not find clear differences by age or family background. Another review found smaller effects overall and almost no difference when reading groups were compared with children doing other active activities, so the size of the benefit is still debated even though its direction against no reading is not. The likely mechanism is the same back-and-forth engine described across this library. Books are a good conversation-holder, because the pictures keep you both looking at the same thing. Reading the same book again and again, a toddler favorite, is fine; familiar books may make it easier for your child to join in.

sources.citation: Dowdall N, Melendez-Torres GJ, Murray L, et al. Shared picture book reading interventions for child language development: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development. 2020;91(2):e383-e399.
sources.role: Meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials: larger effects on expressive than receptive language

sources.citation: Whitehurst GJ, Falco FL, Lonigan CJ, et al. Accelerating language development through picture book reading. Developmental Psychology. 1988;24(4):552-559.
sources.role: The original dialogic reading experiment
